rules.statement: An OAuth client must send its authorization request through Pushed Authorization Requests (RFC 9126) whenever the provider advertises `pushed_authorization_request_endpoint`, and must never fall back to the front channel when PAR is required.
rules.why: If the client could fall back or let the caller pick the channel, a caller could skip PAR.
rules.check: Look for authorization-URL building that uses the front channel even though discovery metadata includes a PAR endpoint, or that falls back to the front channel after PAR is found to be required.

rules.statement: Treat PAR as required when the provider advertises `require_pushed_authorization_requests` or the client registration sets `RequirePushedAuthorizationRequests`. When PAR is required but the provider has no PAR endpoint, throw before sending anything.
rules.why: RFC 9126 §5 and §6 define both the provider flag and the client flag. Sending the request anyway would break the requirement.
rules.check: Check that both flags are read. Check that the missing-endpoint case throws (a provider exception) and doesn't build a front-channel URL or send a request.

rules.statement: Give authorization requests one public entry point that picks the channel itself, and don't add a public push-only API or a caller-selected channel.
rules.why: Otherwise every caller would re-implement the 'PAR required' rule and could skip PAR.
rules.check: Look for new public methods that push only, or a parameter that lets the caller choose between front channel and PAR.

rules.statement: An OAuth client must always send `response_type=code` with PKCE `S256` and must compute `code_challenge` itself from the caller's `code_verifier` as BASE64URL(SHA-256(ASCII(verifier))). It must never accept a challenge or challenge method from the caller.
rules.why: RFC 9700 requires code flow with PKCE. Taking a challenge from the caller would allow `plain` or a challenge that doesn't match the verifier.
rules.check: Look for public request models or parameters that accept `code_challenge` or `code_challenge_method`, for a `plain` method, or for a response_type other than code.

rules.statement: Validate a PKCE `code_verifier` when it is constructed: it must be 43 to 128 characters drawn only from `[A-Za-z0-9-._~]`.
rules.check: Check that the verifier's length and character set are validated where the request object is created or initialized.

rules.statement: When a provider advertises `code_challenge_methods_supported` and the list doesn't include `S256`, fail with a provider exception. When the list is absent, accept the provider.
rules.why: The client only supports S256. A missing list doesn't mean S256 is unsupported.
rules.check: Check the discovery handling: a missing list must not be rejected, and a list without S256 must not be ignored.

rules.statement: Accept extension authorization parameters (`prompt`, `max_age`, `login_hint` and others) through an open additional-parameters dictionary copied with ordinal comparison, not through fixed fields. At `init`, reject with `ArgumentException` empty names and any name the client writes itself or that would break the flow, such as response_type, client_id, redirect_uri, state, nonce, scope, resource, response_mode, code_challenge, code_challenge_method, request_uri, client_secret, client_assertion, client_assertion_type and dpop_jkt.
rules.why: Protocol vocabularies are open. A caller must not be able to override or duplicate parameters the client controls, and DPoP binding belongs to the client.
rules.check: Look for new fixed properties for extension parameters, a dictionary copy that doesn't use StringComparer.Ordinal, or a reserved-name list that misses names the client writes.

rules.statement: In a PAR body, send `client_id` exactly once: add it after client authentication only when the authenticator didn't already add it. Don't add it to token or revocation requests this way.
rules.why: RFC 9126 §2.1 requires `client_id` in the push. `client_secret_basic` puts credentials only in the header, while `private_key_jwt` and `client_secret_post` already add `client_id`, so adding it every time would duplicate it.
rules.check: Look for code that always adds `client_id` to a form body after authentication, or never adds it, without checking what the authenticator already wrote.

rules.statement: Treat a PAR response as successful only when it is `201` with a JSON object whose `request_uri` is a non-empty string and whose `expires_in` is a positive whole number, read with the shared whole-number reader (so `60.0` is accepted). Return an OAuth error object at any status as result data. Throw a provider exception for a `201` missing either field and for anything else.
rules.why: RFC 9126 §2.2 and §2.3 define the response. Whole numbers from a remote party are read strictly through shared readers, and OAuth errors are data, not exceptions.
rules.check: Check the response parsing: accepting 200, accepting an empty `request_uri` or `expires_in` that is zero, negative or has a real fraction, hand-rolled number reading, or throwing on an OAuth error body.

rules.statement: Build the post-PAR authorization URL from `authorization_endpoint` with only `client_id` and `request_uri`. Validate the authorization endpoint before pushing anything, and throw a provider exception when it is missing or unacceptable.
rules.why: RFC 9126 §4 defines the pushed URL. Validating the endpoint first means nothing is pushed when the redirect could never be built.
rules.check: Look for extra parameters added to the pushed URL, or for endpoint validation that happens only after the PAR request has been sent.
